result:
I have been thinking about how cities breathe at night. Not metaphorically, but literally. The exhale of buses, the soft sigh of air conditioners, the occasional cough of a distant train. People say night is quiet, but I think it's just listening at a lower volume.

I walked home last Tuesday after the rain. The streetlights were smeared, halos bleeding into wet asphalt. A kid was selling churros from a cart that smelled like burnt sugar and hope. He didn't try to sell to me, just nodded. I bought one anyway.

There's a particular kind of loneliness that is comfortable. It doesn't demand anything. You sit on a bench, watch the neon flicker, and realize you are exactly where you need to be for now. No epiphany, no crisis. Just a pause.

My phone buzzed three times. I didn't check. Later I saw it was my sister asking if I wanted soup. I said yes. That was the whole conversation.

I think we underestimate small kindnesses. A held door, a shared umbrella, someone remembering your coffee order. These are not grand gestures. They are stitches holding the day together.

The city never sleeps, it just changes shifts. Somewhere a baker is already awake, flour on his forearms. Somewhere a nurse is finishing a round. Somewhere someone is writing something they'll never send.

I am learning to be a good neighbor to myself. To not rush past my own thoughts. To let the night be a night.

Maybe that's enough today.
